explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The voices say, "Come back, come back, O Shulammite! Come back, come back, that we may gaze upon you." (Song of Solomon 6:13) The Shulammite is the young woman of this love poem. That's a whole lot of calling just to get a good look at her.

Not quite, friend. The voices say they want her back "…that we may gaze upon you." (Song of Solomon 6:13) The text gives that one reason and no other. They say it four times, so they are not shy about it.

I see why you'd think so, friend, since most of us describe a person from the top down. This one doesn't. It opens with "How beautiful are your sandaled feet, O daughter of the prince!" (Song of Solomon 7:1) The poet starts at the bottom and climbs.

Right, friend. It starts at her feet: "How beautiful are your sandaled feet, O daughter of the prince!" (Song of Solomon 7:1) Then it works up to her neck, her eyes and her head. It's a trip from the ground to the crown.

That's it, friend. The poem says, "the king is captured in your tresses." (Song of Solomon 7:5) Her hair is like purple threads, and the king is caught right in it. I've been stuck in a junk drawer, but never in anything that pretty.
Not quite, friend. The text says, "the king is captured in your tresses." (Song of Solomon 7:5) The shepherd isn't named in this line. Here it's the king who gets caught.
Good guess, friend. But this verse says, "the king is captured in your tresses." (Song of Solomon 7:5) The watchman isn't named here. The king is the one caught.
Whoa, friend, that's the opposite of what he says. He says, "I will climb the palm tree; I will take hold of its fruit." (Song of Solomon 7:8) He doesn't plan to keep away. He plans to climb.
Yes, friend. The speaker says, "I will climb the palm tree; I will take hold of its fruit." (Song of Solomon 7:8) Nobody here is staying back. This speaker has a plan, and the plan is UP.

explanations.answer: She is his and his desire is for her
explanations.explanation: That's the one. She says, "I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me." (Song of Solomon 7:10) It's short, and she says it plainly. After all that poetry about her, she speaks for herself in one line.

explanations.answer: She must wait for him to return
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd pick it, friend. Here she says something different: "I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me." (Song of Solomon 7:10) No waiting in this line. She says she is his and he wants her.

explanations.answer: She will search the city for him
explanations.explanation: Not this one, friend. In this line she says, "I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me." (Song of Solomon 7:10) She isn't looking for him here. She's telling who she belongs to.

Right, friend. She says, "Come, my beloved, let us go to the countryside; let us spend the night among the wildflowers." (Song of Solomon 7:11) She's the one doing the inviting here. She's the one who asks him to come along.

It's true, friend. Right after her short line, she says, "Come, my beloved, let us go to the countryside; let us spend the night among the wildflowers." (Song of Solomon 7:11) She's the one who asks him to come along.

explanations.answer: If the vine has budded and the blossom opened
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. She wants to see "…if the vine has budded, if the blossom has opened, if the pomegranates are in bloom…" (Song of Solomon 7:12) She names the vine, the blossom and the pomegranates. It's buds and blooms she's watching for.

explanations.answer: If the grapes are ripe and ready to pick
explanations.explanation: That's a good thought, friend, but it isn't what she says. She wants to see "…if the vine has budded, if the blossom has opened…" (Song of Solomon 7:12) It's buds and blossoms she names, not ripe grapes.

explanations.answer: If the vines have been pruned and tied up
explanations.explanation: Pruning is a real job in a vineyard, friend, but it isn't what she mentions. She wants to see "…if the vine has budded, if the blossom has opened, if the pomegranates are in bloom…" (Song of Solomon 7:12) She's watching for blooms, not checking anyone's work.

explanations.answer: Every delicacy she has treasured up for him
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. She says, "…at our door is every delicacy, new as well as old, that I have treasured up for you, my beloved." (Song of Solomon 7:13) She saved up new ones and old ones. That's more planning than I've done for any batch.

explanations.answer: A gift of jewels sent from the king
explanations.explanation: Jewels do show up in this passage, friend. They're in the poem's praise of her thighs, in 7:1. But at the door she says, "…every delicacy, new as well as old, that I have treasured up for you, my beloved." (Song of Solomon 7:13) The gift is from her.

explanations.answer: A message waiting from her brothers
explanations.explanation: Not at this door, friend. She says, "…at our door is every delicacy, new as well as old, that I have treasured up for you, my beloved." (Song of Solomon 7:13) No message is mentioned. It's delicacies she saved for him.

explanations.answer: So she could kiss him outdoors and not be despised
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. She says, "If I found you outdoors, I would kiss you, and no one would despise me." (Song of Solomon 8:1) She wants that kind of ease with him in public. The text gives that as her wish.

explanations.answer: So they could share the family vineyard together
explanations.explanation: A vineyard did come up earlier, friend, but not as the reason here. She says, "If I found you outdoors, I would kiss you, and no one would despise me." (Song of Solomon 8:1) Her wish is about kissing him outdoors without anyone looking down on her.

explanations.answer: So they could inherit their father's land together
explanations.explanation: That's a creative one, friend, but the text doesn't go there. She says, "If I found you outdoors, I would kiss you, and no one would despise me." (Song of Solomon 8:1) Her reason is the kiss, with nobody despising her for it.

That's right, friend. She says, "I would lead you and bring you to the house of my mother who taught me." (Song of Solomon 8:2) Then she adds spiced wine and the nectar of her pomegranates. Her mother's house is where she wants to bring him.

I see how that one slid in, friend, since it's so close to "mother" on the page. But she says, "…the house of my mother who taught me." (Song of Solomon 8:2) No master is mentioned. It's her mother's house.

The king does turn up in this passage, friend. He's the one caught in her tresses in 7:5. But in 8:2 she says, "…the house of my mother who taught me." It's her mother's house she wants to take him to.
